Why I switched editors (and why you probably shouldn't)

November 2, 2026

For eleven years I used the same text editor. I knew its quirks the way you know the creaks of an old house, and I had a configuration file long enough to qualify as a short novel. Last spring, almost on a whim, I moved to something new, and this is the story of how that went, what I gained, and what I quietly miss.

The first week was humbling. Muscle memory is a strange thing: my fingers kept reaching for shortcuts that no longer existed, and every small slip reminded me how much of my work happened below the level of conscious thought. I had assumed that switching tools would be a technical exercise, a matter of mapping old commands to new ones, but it turned out to be closer to moving to a new city.

What surprised me most was not what the new editor did better, although it did several things better. It was how much the change made me notice my own habits. I had been doing certain things a certain way for so long that I had forgotten they were choices at all. Some of those choices were good ones. Others were workarounds for problems that had been solved years ago.

So should you switch? Probably not, at least not for the reasons I did. If your tools feel invisible, that is a sign they are working. The best editor is the one that gets out of your way, and the cost of a switch is paid in attention, which is the one thing most of us cannot spare. But if you find yourself fighting your tools every day, it might be worth a look around, if only to remember that the way you work is something you get to decide.

In the end I am glad I switched, mostly because it reminded me that comfort and quality are not the same thing. Whether I will still feel that way in another eleven years is a question for a later essay.
